We had a problem as far as locating the command where Visnjevo was concerned because the Sipreski Battalion used to be located in Visnjevo and we had a problem down in Mehurici because previously, and I don't know on whose authorisation, there was the -- there was some foreigners who were present there in addition to the TO detachment. So if the command of the battalion was to be located in Mehurici and if we were to provide some of the men with accommodation there -- since they didn't have their families or their homes in those areas, some of them just had nothing -- we had to find accommodation for them, too. And then it was necessary to remove those foreigners. They had to liberate those premises so that the command of the battalion could be located there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: The Chamber's indulgence. If I'm following my friend right I think she's dealing with the document 531 dated the 20th of December. Am I correct? I'm not sure if we are still on the same document. I think I am lost.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness recognised the document and he said that this was one of the problems that they encountered. Now he is speaking about other problems that are not linked to that document, but rather these problems are linked to the problems that the 306th Brigade had. So these answers, these problems, are not ones that concern this document. You mentioned facilities and barracks, Mr. Siljak --

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: May I interrupt. But I think the document speaks of the organisational structure, and it seems to me we have gone much wider than that. We are not talking now about the organisational structure as such, now their location, where they were housed, their barracks, and I'm not sure if that is appropriate with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think you have understood me well. The document was shown to the witness. When the witness finished answering questions about organisational problems, three documents were shown and I have moved on to another subject. I asked about other problems that arose when 306th Brigade was being formed. If I haven't been clear enough, I could try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Trial Chamber is following you very well. Please go ahead, especially since interesting issues have been raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said that facilities for command were, on the whole, schools, and you spoke about the location of these commands and about the school in Mehurici. Can you tell us where the men were, where the soldiers were, with the exception of the Sipreski Battalion composed of refugees located in the school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: Our soldiers, those who were at the positions facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor, that's where they were and the other soldiers were at home because they didn't have barracks. So when they weren't at positions, they remained at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what sort of skilled staff did the 306th Brigade and its units have at the time of its formation and up until mid-1993?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: Well, I usually like to use myself as an example when I address an issue. First of all, I was appointed as the chief of staff, and as far as educational background is concerned, I had completed secondary school, teacher training school. I had completed a school for reserve officers. This course in Bileca lasted four months and I trained in Turbe. So while doing my military service I was trained as a platoon commander. I had the rank of captain first class in the former JNA. And on the basis of my educational background and my military knowledge I was not fit for the post I was assigned. Esid Sipic, my commander, was a commander of Karaula somewhere in Slovenia, in the JNA. That's what he said. He was a senior officer -- he was a senior sergeant. I don't know whether he completed this later on, but he had a -- he was given the possibility of forming a brigade, of commanding a brigade. The other members of the command, although quite a few of them who didn't have military or specialist knowledge, there was some reserve officers who had never even come across the sort of tasks they had to carry out that time. And I could first mention the assistant for organisation, mobilisation and his official. They had never been involved in such work before but now they had to do this. Then the chief of communications in the brigade command was a senior sergeant who certainly couldn't have taken stock of the situation, but he was a reserve staff sergeant; he wasn't an active one. The battalion commanders were active duty officers. They had finished the military academy and I thought they would provide us with significant assistance, but they were very young and they had only just graduated from the military academy so that they were not sufficiently prepared for the tasks they were assigned. They were either commanders of platoons or commanders of companies in the former JNA. Now they were appointed as battalion commanders and given the task of establishing battalions. As for the companies we didn't have a single active-duty officer in companies, we didn't have an active duty company command or active duty assistants. But these were people who had gained a certain reputation in the villages, people who could be leaders. But I won't even mention the problem of commanders of detachments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what sort of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: Well, as I said at the beginning, we received about a hundred barrels at the beginning, and when this is shared out among the Territorial Defence in Travnik municipality, and if you try to give each unit at least some weapons, this amounts to a very insignificant amount of weapons. When the warehouse was blown up, when it was being left by members of the former JNA, when they blew it up, one couldn't say all the weapons were destroyed, that's impossible. Some weapons remained. The explosion had thrown them at some distance, but some individuals would go to the warehouse; they would gather weapons or ammunition for themselves. There was some rifles that had been burned. There were rifles with faults, but they were used. Weapons that people bought on the black market were also used. They would buy these weapons for themselves. Hunting weapons. 306th Brigade were also used, I think. Sometime at the beginning of February when we were taking stock of the situation we realised we had between 500 and 600 barrels, various sorts of weapons, hunting weapons, military weapons that were -- functioned correctly or had faults.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at the next document, the document listed under number 5 in your file. This is Defence number 0730. Can you tell me if you recognise this document, and if you do to comment. So if you do recognise the document, can you please comment on some of the points in this document.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: This document was drafted by the instruction and training body. I do recognise it because this organ was in direct communication with the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the text under 1(A). This column under 1 to 13, what is it?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: As you can see from the document, it indicates the situation in the unit, what the replenishment situation of the units was on the 11th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, and my apologies in advance if this sounds like a leading question, but your 306th Brigade on this date did not have enough men, that it was not replenished to full strength.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: The 306th Mountain Brigade not only on this date, never -- was never replenished with appropriate number of troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Information under 1(B), the total that we see here 572. Was that reflect what you just indicated, the total number of weapons that you had at your disposal at the time?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: Yes. This is exactly what the document confirms. It confirms what I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, I should like to hear your comment on the assessment of the situation with the weapons and the difficulties in taking possession of this area. Now, the information indicated here, does it correspond to the actual situation as it was familiar to you in 1993?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: This is perhaps an understatement because we hesitated to inform the command of how band the situation was in the field. The situation was very complex indeed, and the information contained here is definitely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, I would like to finish with this document. A moment ago you indicated for us on the map all of the villages in the Biljanska Valley. You also showed us the area on the model. Can you now tell us what the composition of the population was in your area. And in connection to that, did additional problems arise concerning the formation of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: A moment ago when I spoke about the villages of the Biljanska Valley, I said that the Croat villages were not located in one single area, nor was that the case with the Bosniak villages. I could perhaps indicate for you on the map what specific villages were Bosniak, what were Croat, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please do that for us.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: What one should bear in mind and what I should perhaps start with is the fact that the upper part of the Bila River was inhabited by predominantly Bosniak villages -- Gluha Bukovica, Visnjevo, Dub, Orahovo, Zagradje, Skomorje, Mehurici, Suhi Dol. Now, Suhi Dol was not a purely Bosniak village. Part of the population was Serb. The same situation was in Poljanice. It was a predominantly Bosniak village with several Serb households. Fazlici was a Bosniak village. Jezerci also and between Jezerci and Zagradje, there was a hamlet of Miletici where the majority population was Croat with three to four Bosniak households. Going further down, down the Bila River, we come across the Croat village of Postinje, Puselje, and Matici. And on the right bank of the Bila, you have the village of Malinje. Gornji Malinje is inhabited by Croats and Donji Malinje by Bosniaks. Now, since I'm here on the right bank of the Bila let me mention Guca Gora, which is a Croat village. Krpeljici. There is a small Croat population there, however the majority is Bosniak. To the north-west of Krpeljici we come across the village of Radonjici, also predominantly Croat. South of Radonjici there are two hamlets, Velika Bukovica and Mala Bukovica. Vela Bukovica is Bosniak and Mala Bukovica is Croat. Now, these Vela Bukovica and Mala Bukovica, the names of the villages are misleading because Mala Bukovica is actually larger than Velika Bukovica in terms of number of residents. To the east of Bukovica we find the village of Mosor. Mosor is a Bosniak village and to the south-east of Mosor there is the village of Bandol, partly Bosniak, partly Croat. Radojcici, north-east of Bandol, is inhabited by Bosniak population. Let me now finish with the right bank of the Bila and then I will go back to this area here. The villages of Banovici and Sarici are inhabited by Croats. The village of Zolote, Alihodze, and Karahodze are Bosniak villages. If we continue, we come across the village of Pokrajcici and neighbouring hamlets, which is a Croat village. The town of Stara Bila is located at the mouth of the River Bila into the River Lasva, which area is inhabited by Croats. On this side, in this area here, I think I should also mention the village of Brankovac. Now, in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this village which was also referred to by Bosniaks as Ricice, only a small portion of the population was Bosniak and all other villages in the area were inhabited by Croats. Let me now go back to --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to indicate interesting places on the other side as well when you're indicating on the map, so as not to lose too much time. I know all these villages are significant but later on we will be only interested in the locations linked with the events contained in the indictment. So can you show us only those villages that are of interest in terms of the position and the positions of the 306th Brigade when you move to this other side.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: It is very difficult to choose what to show because the villages here are like leopard skin, but let me give it a try. Cukle, for instance, is located on the border with the Zenica municipality. Part of the village, the hamlet of Softici, is inhabited by Bosniaks. The remainder of the population is Croat. Novo Selo is located right on the border between the Travnik and Zenica municipalities. This area is sometimes referred to as Ovnak because of the vicinity of the Ovnak Pass, the mountain pass. This village a Croat village, just as Grahovcici, which I'm indicating now. On the road leading to Zenica, we find the village of Brajkovici which is a predominantly Croat village with only the part towards Han Bila being inhabited by Bosniaks. The road going alongside the Bila, that is from Han Bila onwards, on the portion of the road where we see the words "Dolac" and "Baje" where the command of the 306th was located, now, in this area Baje are inhabited by Croats, whereas Dolac by Bosniaks. We also have the village of Kljaci, a Bosniak village on this bank of the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. If later on it turns out to be necessary to indicate more villages, we will ask you to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now have a recess and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give you the floor, let me remind you of the time. We have one hour left and tomorrow only three hours and 45 minutes. If you do not manage to finish tomorrow, unfortunately the witness will have to stay until Tuesday. So either you speed up and we're able to finish tomorrow -- but given the speed, the rhythm, so far I am not sure. You have asked for six hours. If six hours are then needed for cross-examination, it's then not two days only but longer than that because six hours, if we take into account the breaks, it's not two days but at least four days. And I think that there are two witnesses scheduled for six to eight hours. All others are one to two hours. So now we really have a problem. If the testimony is not completed, the witness will have to stay for additional three days, minimum, or you really have to speed up the examination. Now let me hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I take note of what you say. Yesterday evening we indicated that the Defence would examine this witness within the envisaged six hours. We're really very sorry that yesterday's witness stayed longer than expected; after all, he was the first one. And we really hoped that Remzija Siljak would appear right after that. We will definitely try to finish within six hours. I will try to shorten the testimony, but it will be not longer than for 30 minutes. Whether we are going to finish tomorrow I don't know. It will be up to the Prosecution and the Chamber to make the best use of their time for the questions for this witness. But it is very important for us to complete the examination of the witness within the envisaged time framework.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, before the break you spoke about the problems of the composition of the population which effected the activity of the 306th Brigade. Earlier you indicated that in one of the buildings where the battalion command was located there were also foreigners. What happened with those foreigner later on? Did they remain in the building where the command of your battalion was located?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: In order to carry on the transfer of this battalion, that is the people from Visnjevo to the Mehurici school, the foreigners left the school premises. I myself wasn't present in there, but I think that they left behind two to three offices which were full of their equipment. So yes. Physically they were no longer present in this building, but they would come back from time to time to these offices to get their things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where they went?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: They took up quarters in the village of Poljanice, not far from Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies, my colleague has drawn my attention to the French interpretation. Apparently the French interpretation was that three officers remained behind; however, the witness said that three offices were left empty. So if the remark of my colleague is correct, I kindly ask that the transcript be corrected. Sorry, I interrupted you. What happened with those foreigners?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: They moved to the village of Poljanice and took up quarters in some barns and houses that had been occupied by Serb families. So they established a kind of camp there. I never went there. It was impossible to go there. They didn't allow anyone near their camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, the presence of these foreigners in the area where elements of your brigade were deployed, did that presence create problems for your brigade in the area where you were, and if so what kind of problems were there?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: Yes. There were problems, first of all, because of the fact that part of the troops from that area, regardless of the fact that pursuant to this order that I mentioned were supposed to become members of the 306th Brigade went to them. Now, when I say that they went to them, I have to explain. Now, one must admit that part of the population, when they foreigners arrived, accepted them in the beginning wholeheartedly, because after all they had come to help the people in this area. However, later when they started calling up young men to join their ranks, they were able to offer them some payment in kind and even some salaries. And those who did not want to go to the line, towards the Serbian aggressor, preferred to go to these foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I think there is another very important mistake. Page 65 [as interpreted], line 24 which says that part of the troops from the area went to them. You spoke about individuals. You spoke about persons. Who went to see them? Who went to them -- went over to them?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: I said that because some able-bodied men who pursuant to the order of the command of the 3rd Corps of the replenishment of the 306th Brigade were supposed to join the 306th Brigade didn't go to the 306th Brigade but went over to them, because they gave them weapons, clothes, all sorts of parcels and even sometimes payment in kind. One other reason why these young men prefer to go over to them was because they didn't go to the front line against the Serbs. So in order to avoid service in the ranks of the 306th Brigade and being deployed on the line towards the Serbs, they went over to these foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the presence of these foreigners create other problems in connection with the local population? And were there inhabitants who accepted their presence in the area for some other reasons?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: A moment ago I started about -- with explaining what other problems there were. Yes, there were problems with the local population because the foreigners who had come to this area practiced their religion in a different way, the so-called Mesud, which is completely different than the kind of service that is normally performed in the area. And those who were not willing to accept this new type of service had problems. So these villages experienced division amongst their own population because some of the residents had accepted this new type of religious service because they thought after all because of the fact that these foreigners spoke very good Arabic they must be right. Whereas others continued with the usual type of service. So, for instance, a mosque would be divided according to the types of service practiced.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me who these people are, the people who did not accept this. Were they inhabitants, soldiers, or other people? You mentioned people who accepted this and others who didn't.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: I was speaking about the population of the Bila area. As far as I know their arrival had an effect on the wide area, but I am sure that they had an effect on the Bila area. I know that there were problems in the village where I was born, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have referred to a number of significant problems that occurred at the time of formation of the brigade, could you tell me in what manner the brigade command attempted to establish command and control and to what extent was it in contact with the superior command, and what measures were taken to train and fill up your brigade. To what extent was this possible? It's a broad question but try and answer it.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: As I said, after those problems at the beginning in relation to the formation of the brigade when we returned to the idea of formation on the basis of territory, that is to say when a battalion is formed from a detachment and when the brigade started functioning in this manner, we then tried to make use of the existing infrastructure, of the existing communications, in order to link up with battalion commands -- not with the barracks, but with the places where battalion commands were located. The communication lines were never very reliable and even before, the Bila Valley was quite far away from the centre of Travnik; there weren't that many telephone lines in that area. A small exchange was set up, but it was overburdened. So one could never be sure of having a telephone line or having communication lines. This wire line passed through Travnik and villages where there were Croats and villages where there are Bosniaks, too. In this sense it was not reliable either. As far as other equipment is concerned, we used former JNA equipment. That would be an RUP-12 radio device. We had a WW device for communications with the superior command. But such devices require a source of power. They require spare parts. So at the beginning we thought that we would be able to cope to a certain extent, that the situation with regard to communications equipment would improve, but it deteriorated because we were short of batteries, we didn't have sources of energy for these devices. And if a device was faulty we didn't have any spare parts and it was impossible to use these communication means. Couriers were the best way to maintain communications because of the configuration of the land. That is to say, the roads that were used if there were any excess situations with the HVO, these roads could no longer be used [as interpreted]. They were no longer safe. So it was difficult to use couriers, too. Within the brigade, where the brigade was located, we tried to have good communication lines on the line towards the Serbian aggressor. So the communications, the lines themselves, were ones that were supposed to be good and we had good communication lines up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the brigade command, and the 3rd Corps command, did you take any measure to train soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we have a technical problem. We are unable to see or understand the question that is posed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, nothing appears in the transcript. The transcript doesn't reflect what we are speaking of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the technical booth. I'm told the technician will arrive in one minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps we could make this use. After the questions I intend to put now, I would like to ask the witness if he could mark the positions of the BH army units, and the 306th Brigade positions of HVO units and Serbian forces. While waiting for the technician to deal with this problem, he could perhaps indicate this on the map. He could draw them on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be best for him to indicate these positions in order to save time and then as soon as the problem has been solved, we will take care of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, could you please point on the map to the positions of the 306th Brigade and the positions of BH army units in the Bila Valley at the end of May 1993. Could you point to the positions of the HVO. This will make it easier for me to put further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: Just one technical question. What colour should I use to mark these positions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Use blue for the BH army, red for the Republika Srpska forces, and green for the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's working now, so we no longer have a problem. Please go ahead. If the technician could zoom in. It's a pity I can't use the controls myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked the witness to do this now because tomorrow, if I have understood the situation correctly, we'll be in Courtroom II and we can only use the map in the courtroom. We won't be able to use the model. Have I understood this correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow means tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Courtroom II. So the map will have to be moved there. The registrar will take care of that, not alone of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the lines of the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. In this part of the Vlasic plateau I have indicated a wider area. There is the zone of responsibility of the 312th. And this will enable me to mark the adjacent unit, the position of an adjacent unit. These were the defence lines held by the 306th facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor before those conflicts that broke out, or rather before the 31st of May, 1993. This is the zone of responsibility where the 306th was present, but I have added this, too, because it's one whole and this is where the HVO held the lines. And as I said a while ago, we had army forces here facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. And here in Rakic and Krnjevo and there was a forward security post in Rajkovici held by the HVO. I personally visited these areas, since when we cooperated, before problems arose, I passed through these lines, so I know about their location. And the depth, do you want me to indicate the positions in the depth, too? I said that one battalion of the 306th, or rather its command post was in the village of Visnjevo. The 4th Battalion was there. The 2nd Battalion of the 306th, the battalion command, was in the village of Krpeljici. The third battalion, its command post was in Han Bila. And the 1st Battalion was in the school in Mehurici. These were the battalions in the forward command post of the 306th facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor was in the area of Paric Greda in a hut. The brigade command was located in the premises, in the facilities of the Bila mine, that concerns these units. In Mehurici some of the men from that battalion were located there. Some of the men from the 1st Battalion were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Page 65 line 14 it says that the battalion was at the forward command post. That's what the transcript says. In fact it's line 15. These were the battalions at the forward command post. The witness said that there was a forward command post that existed towards the Serbian Montenegrin aggressor. There was a number of officers from the brigade command and they had servicemen who were there. They were part of the military police platoon intended to provide security for the command post and there was some people who were there to prepare food and there were officers, too. Could you please indicate the positions of the HVO now.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: The positions of the HVO in the Bila Valley? Well, I have already drawn or indicated where some of the men were at the positions facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. In Guce Gora there was the command of the Frankopan Brigade. That's where the command of that Frankopan Brigade was located and the command of a battalion was there. I don't know which one, but it was a battalion from the Frankopan Brigade. Other men from the Frankopan Brigade were deployed in the villages -- well, I don't know how to draw it. But one unit was in Cukle and there was another unit in Grahovcici. As far as the strength of these units are concerned, according to the information I had at the time and the estimates that were made at the time, or the estimates we received from the intelligence organs, here they had the strength of one company and here there was a unit strength of one battalion. But after the events in Zenica, part of the Jure Francetic Brigade from Zenica was relocated here in this area. Here of Novo Selo and Grahovcici, we had some men from the Jure Francetic Brigade there. We had part of the Jure Francetic Brigade located there. I'll mark legitimate JF for Jure Francetici. Nova Bila, well, I would prefer to draw a line here which would enable you to see the territory that was exclusively Croatian territory and territory where it wasn't possible to pass through. It was under the complete control of the HVO. I will also indicate this area which was under the control of the BH republic army and no one else could pass through that area without some sort of a joint agreement having been reached, or if there was a crisis situation, checkpoints would be moved on both sides. So in -- when there was a crisis, because the 31st of May was a crisis of sorts, at the permanent checkpoint -- there was a permanent checkpoint, it was never removed even when there was a crisis. There was an HVO checkpoint in the area of this crossroads in Ovnak. That's the checkpoint here, and it was on the road leading from Zenica, Han Bila, onwards to Mehurici or rather via Guca Gora to Han Bila. As I lived in Travnik at that time and I would go to the commands or to the 306th Brigade, there was a checkpoint at the exit from Travnik in the area that we called Kanare and I'd indicate this position on the map by saying that it's north from Gradac. There is this crossroads and there is road that turns off towards Guca Gora. It's on the Travnik-Vitez road. And it is this checkpoint here which was an HVO checkpoint. What is very important -- it is very important for this zone of responsibility because it wasn't possible to go to Zenica or Travnik without permission to pass through these checkpoints. And then a checkpoint which was occasionally set up, because there were permanent checkpoints and there were temporary ones, there was a checkpoint here at Okuka. And I think that there wasn't a soul who wasn't aware of this checkpoint in the municipality of Travnik. It was frequently discussed, but it was never removed and it wasn't set up on a joint basis. It was this checkpoint on Okuka. Again, you control the routes to Novi Travnik and Vitez and other areas. Temporary checkpoints, and I know this because I had an unpleasant experience myself because as chief of staff, although I had permission from the Frankopan Brigade to take a computer to Travnik to be repaired, although I had such permission, there was a group that had organised itself at this temporary checkpoint. And this wasn't a rare appearance, because in our brigade there were frequent complaints with regard to this pass. My computer was taken from me at this checkpoint. It was a computer used by the brigade command. It was taken away by men at the checkpoint. They more or less allowed us to pass through, but they took the computer for themselves. So those are the checkpoints I have mentioned. Now let me also mention the Bosniak side, the BH republic army or the Travnik public security station. The Travnik public security station, or rather the police station at Mehurici, had a checkpoint at the entrance to Mehurici at the location I have marked. So you could say that this area from this checkpoint here, Poljanice, Suhi Dol, and then you could say from Suhi Dol further upwards, you could say that this area was under the complete control of the BH republic army. This includes the villages of Jezerci and this northeastern part of Travnik municipality. The villages down here, well, I'd like to show you how complicated the situation was. I'd like to do so. I don't know if I will succeed but I would like to do this for the sake of the truth, because it was difficult for the Bosniak population as they felt surrounded, and it was difficult for the Croatian population, too. Cukle. It's a bit difficult to use this felt tip. This part of the village of Cukle. In Softici it has been marked in blue. Softici is a village inhabited by Muslims. Everything around here is inhabited by Croats. I'll extend this line because it also covered Mrkonje, Alibasici. This part was inhabited by Croats. In this part, in the lower part of Cukle -- it's called Drinak, but you can't see the name on the map -- a small group of Muslims lived here. And in this part here as you can see there were Muslims and they constantly complained and they were always in some sort of danger or their lives were always threatened. That is what they thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Siljak, when marking the locations on the map, could you perhaps move a little bit to the right so that the camera can record and everyone can see what you are saying and drawing.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: It is slightly difficult for me, because when I draw a line or mark a position it gets rubbed out later. I marked the battalion command, but it's no longer there; it's been smudged. Let me continue. The Croatian -- the village of Orasac was also inhabited by Croats. The village of Puselje is also a Croatian area. Between Cukle and Orasac there is a small Muslim village called Vranici. And then we have Podovi, or Pode. This is an area of Muslim villages and it links up with Han Bila. Maline, as I have said, it's inhabited by both Muslims in Donji Maline. It's a mixed village and I'm drawing this because at that time for these people each of these villages was a sort of front in itself. It wasn't possible to move from here and no one wanted to leave because no one wanted to leave the villages and go to the lines facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor, because their families could be endangered. I also mentioned Krpeljici, with a minority Croatian population. Then there's Mala Bukovica and Mosor, part of the village of Bandol, Radonjici. I mentioned Han Bila and then Zolote, Brajici and Alihodze. I'll encircle all of these villages because they form one whole. And then the line continues to the villages of Dolac and Knjaci. These are the last villages in this part. And I also said in this part in the area of Brankovac there was a village inhabited by some Muslims. I said up here this was an area inhabited just by Muslims. What about the Croatian part? Let me start with Mala Bukovica. Mala Bukovica was a Croat village; Radonjici, another Croat village; Gornji Maline and Bikosi, also Croat; Postinje, which is linked up with Matici and Puselje; also inhabited by Croats, Guca Gora; part of Bandol, linked up with the area of Brizenje [phoen] and Kule; Cifluk. Brankovac got erased in the meantime. So all of this area here that I'm now going to mark -- Pestovici, Pokrajcici -- is linked up with Zabile, part of Zadavici [phoen] and Stara Bila. This whole area here that I'm indicated is inhabited by Croat population. Puticevo and on to Putac. This area, too, is a Croat area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down. Now, the map was filmed so that we can use it for questions later on. We spoke about links in communications and I would like to finish with that part by the end of the hearing today. So in relation to that, let us have a look at the document entitled "Formation of the 306th Brigade" under number 6, 7, 8, and 9. Tell me, please, do you recognise these documents? Do they indicate the problems that you had with formation of this brigade and the steps taken in order to solve these problems?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise all of these documents. Document under number 6 is an order of the 3rd Corps command. For the purposes of getting insight, in light of the assessment of the situation there the commander of the corps ordered that teams be formed, teams that will tour the units and acquaint themselves with the structure of the units and the level of organisation and formation of the units, and as far as I remember, as part of the formation of operations groups within the 3rd Corps. It was at that time that the OGs within the 3rd Corps were formed and the commanders were to tour the units and familiarise themselves with the situation there. But the command of the 3rd Corps also found it necessary that a team be dispatched into the field to take stock of the situation. The 306th was within the OG Zapad at the time. As far as I know one such team went there and the commander of the OG West inspected the troops that were not deployed on the lines at that time and the team filed or sent a report, after which we received an order that deficiencies be removed and the problems that we had identified be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Document number 7, please.

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: Number 7 is an order that I received as an individual. This order appointed me to the position of the chief of staff, but this is not a final order. This is just an order of the staff of the supreme command of the 12th of March, 1993, so four or five months after the formation of the brigade. Here I am appointed as acting chief of staff because the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was authorised to issue an order to that effect. Document number 8 is what I spoke about a moment ago. The feedback, the team dispatched by the command of the 3rd Corps, did identify certain problems. Maybe they ignored some of the problems that we had at the beginning where the units were being formed, but now they are more specific and they are ordering us to carry out the replenishment of the units and equipment in accordance with the appropriate regulations through the secretariat of the Territorial Defence acting in the territory of Travnik municipality. So these would be the relevant documents for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Document number 9?

utterances.speaker: REMZIJA SILJAK
utterances.text: As part of the assessment of the situation in our units, the command of the 306th dispatched their people, their teams, with the task to assess the situation and in an effort to resolve the problems. So this is another report of the inspection on the ground with the assignments signed by the commander of the 306th. This was drafted by an operations officer from the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the name of the officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now move to your relationship with the HVO in the area where HVO units and BH army units were active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have only a little time left maybe it is better to move on to that issue tomorrow. I think it will be more coherent. Sir, as you have heard, you will have to come back tomorrow at 9.00. Tomorrow the hearing will start at 9.00, and in case your testimony is not finished tomorrow at 1345, you will have to come back and appear on Tuesday afternoon, which will probably necessitate your remaining in The Hague over the weekend, unless the Defence is able to speed up tomorrow and the Prosecution does not take up all -- too long for the cross-examination. Is there any problem with your remaining in The Hague over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have come here to tell you what I know about. I don't have any specific commitments because, after all, I am retired. I would like to finish tomorrow because I arrived on Saturday. However, if it is necessary for me to stay longer than that, I am prepared to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I am counting on the ability of the Defence to be succinct and we hope that the witness will not have to stay in The Hague but will be able to go back to his country and his family. We will see tomorrow -- I will see tomorrow how much time we will need for additional questions. I am now going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. You are now under oath. You are not allowed to see anyone until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have a few minutes left. Does the Defence wish to inform us on how the situation will evolve tomorrow? You have heard what our concerns are.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as I have informed you a moment ago, I had scheduled examination of this witness for six hours. In view of the developments in this -- during this week for the reasons that we are all familiar with, I shall endeavour to shorten my examination for about 30 minutes. I still have two subjects left for tomorrow, which subjects are contained in the summary, namely the relationship with the HVO which escalated into a conflict in June; and individual events to the extent the witness is aware of them, the events connected to Maline and Guca Gora. I also intend to show a few documents to the witness in connection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, do you have -- or Ms. Benjamin, do you have any idea about the duration of the cross-examination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution will be dealing very certainly with the first three hours of this testimony today so it will leave us with the latter two paragraphs. And I do not anticipate we will go an hour, an hour and a half. So I believe if my friends were to keep to their word, I think we can get out of here tomorrow. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, we hope that we will be able to finish tomorrow because, as we have heard, the witness would prefer to finish tomorrow. Are there any other questions? Yes, Counsel. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just wish to remind you that we will probably have a few questions for this witness but not longer than 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We take note of that. You need half an hour. Of course we understand that. It is almost 7.00. We are now going to resume until tomorrow 9.00.
